investigation.title: Remote Agent Pod Unschedulable: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity on Swarm Cluster
investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api with an identical Kubernetes scheduler message: the 6-node cluster has zero available slots for new kata peer-pod VMs — 2 nodes report Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm and 4 nodes do not match the pod's node affinity/selector. Because no pod was ever scheduled, the eval runner never received a VM ID or a remote agent state, leaving all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) absent and causing the expected-output contract to fail completely.
investigation.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agents swarm has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource quota on the 2 nodes that carry that resource. The remaining 4 nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity/selector rules. With 0/6 nodes schedulable and preemption unable to free capacity, every attempt to provision a remote agent pod times out unscheduled (~142–143 s), preventing the eval runner from obtaining a VM ID or observing any agent lifecycle state. This is a cluster-capacity or resource-quota exhaustion failure localized to the kata peer-pod runtime tier, not an eval infrastructure or code defect.

possibleCauses: Primary — kata.peerpods.io/vm resource exhaustion: the 2 peer-pod-capable nodes have reached their maximum concurrent VM count. All existing remote agent VMs are consuming the full quota, leaving no capacity for new pods.

Secondary — node affinity/selector misconfiguration or drift: the 4 remaining nodes do not satisfy the pod's node selector, possibly because a label was removed, a node was cordoned/drained, or a taint was added, reducing the schedulable pool from 6 to 2 nodes and making capacity exhaustion more likely.

Tertiary — leaked or zombie remote agent VMs not being cleaned up: if prior eval runs or user sessions left VMs running without releasing the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource, the quota would be consumed faster than expected.
Lower confidence — transient cluster event (node restart, upgrade, or scale-down) temporarily reducing the number of peer-pod-capable nodes below the threshold needed to absorb a new pod.

investigation.title: published-observability-snapshot Eval Fail: Snapshot Age 303 min Exceeds 300 min Contract Limit
investigation.summary: The eval for the published-observability-snapshot check failed because the snapshot at https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json was 303 minutes old at eval time, exceeding the contract's hard maximum of 300 minutes (snapshotAgeMinutes max: 300, as defined in infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json line 482). This is an isolated eval-layer staleness violation; all three sibling public-website checks passed, and no user-traffic or incident signals are present in the evidence.
investigation.rootCause: The GitHub Actions workflow responsible for regenerating and publishing the observability snapshot at https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json did not run within the required 300-minute window. When the eval executed at 2026-07-05T04:28:37Z, the snapshot was already 303 minutes old — 3 minutes past the contract threshold. The snapshot itself is structurally valid (all other assertions pass: schemaVersion=1, source=github-actions, hasLiveSource=true, hasNonUnknownFeatureData=true, featureCount=19), so the failure is exclusively a freshness/scheduling issue, not a data-quality or pipeline-output defect. No user-facing outage is evidenced; this check is marked required=false with statusImpact=informational in the feature registry.
proof: failed-check.message: 'snapshotAgeMinutes expected <= 300 but got 303' — the sole violated assertion is the max-age bound (infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json line 482: { "path": "snapshotAgeMinutes", "max": 300 }).

failed-check.evidence: snapshotAgeMinutes=303, maxAgeMinutes=300, source=github-actions, hasLiveSource=true, hasNonUnknownFeatureData=true, featureCount=19, unknownFeatureCount=0 — all non-age assertions are satisfied, confirming the snapshot content is valid but stale.
expected-output.contract: The contract asserts snapshotAgeMinutes max 300 (infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json line 482). The observed value of 303 directly violates this single assertion.

source.infra/evals/status/features.json:383: The registry entry marks this check as required=false and statusImpact=informational, scoping the impact to an informational eval failure, not a service outage.

sibling.public-observability-page, sibling.public-models-page, sibling.public-marketing-pages: All three sibling checks passed with HTTP 200 responses, confirming the public website itself is reachable and the failure is isolated to snapshot freshness.

source-context.infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs:2168-2173: The runner fetches the snapshot via publicJsonUrl(args.publishedSnapshotUrl) and derives snapshotAgeMinutes from the payload, meaning the age value reflects the actual published file's timestamp, not an eval instrumentation artifact.
failed-check.timing: latencyMs=75 — the probe completed successfully and quickly, ruling out a network or fetch timeout as the cause of the failure.
possibleCauses: Most likely — GitHub Actions workflow scheduling delay or missed run: The snapshot source is github-actions (failed-check.evidence). A workflow that was delayed, queued, or skipped would leave the previously published snapshot in place, causing the age to drift past 300 minutes. The 3-minute overage (303 vs 300) is consistent with a workflow that ran slightly late or was delayed by runner queue pressure.

Less likely — GitHub Actions workflow run failed or was cancelled: If the scheduled workflow failed mid-run or was cancelled, the snapshot would not be updated, producing the same staleness symptom. The snapshot content quality (hasLiveSource=true, hasNonUnknownFeatureData=true) does not rule this out, as those fields reflect the last successful publish.

Less likely — GitHub Pages propagation delay: Even if the workflow ran on time, a GitHub Pages CDN propagation delay could cause the eval to read a stale cached version of status.json. The 3-minute margin makes this plausible but less probable than a scheduling slip.

Least likely — Contract threshold too tight relative to workflow cadence: The feature registry sets staleAfterMinutes=360 for this check, but the expected-output contract enforces maxAgeMinutes=300. If the workflow is scheduled at exactly 300-minute intervals, any minor scheduling jitter will cause the eval to fail. This is a configuration tension, not a runtime failure, but it could explain recurring marginal failures.

investigations.title: Remote Agent Pod Unschedulable: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity on Swarm Cluster
investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api with an identical Kubernetes scheduler message: the 6-node cluster has zero available slots for new kata peer-pod VMs — 2 nodes report Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm and 4 nodes do not match the pod's node affinity/selector. Because no pod was ever scheduled, the eval runner never received a VM ID or a remote agent state, leaving all four required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) absent and causing the expected-output contract to fail completely.
investigations.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agents swarm has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource quota on the 2 nodes that carry that resource. The remaining 4 nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity/selector rules. With 0/6 nodes schedulable and preemption unable to free capacity, every attempt to provision a remote agent pod times out unscheduled (~142–143 s), preventing the eval runner from obtaining a VM ID or observing any agent lifecycle state. This is a cluster-capacity or resource-quota exhaustion failure localized to the kata peer-pod runtime tier, not an eval infrastructure or code defect.

investigations.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agent swarm has exhausted its kata.peerpods.io/vm resource across the 2 eligible nodes (0/2 available, no preemption victims found). This is an eval-observed infrastructure capacity failure localized to the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource pool; no user-traffic or incident signals are present in the supplied evidence.

investigations.rootCause: The GitHub Actions workflow responsible for regenerating and publishing the observability snapshot at https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json did not run within the required 300-minute window. When the eval executed at 2026-07-05T04:28:37Z, the snapshot was already 303 minutes old — 3 minutes past the contract threshold. The snapshot itself is structurally valid (all other assertions pass: schemaVersion=1, source=github-actions, hasLiveSource=true, hasNonUnknownFeatureData=true, featureCount=19), so the failure is exclusively a freshness/scheduling issue, not a data-quality or pipeline-output defect. possibleCauses: Most likely — GitHub Actions workflow scheduling delay or missed run: The snapshot source is github-actions (failed-check.evidence). A workflow that was delayed, queued, or skipped would leave the previously published snapshot in place, causing the age to drift past 300 minutes. The 3-minute overage (303 vs 300) is consistent with a workflow that ran slightly late or was delayed by runner queue pressure.

Less likely — GitHub Actions workflow run failed or was cancelled: If the scheduled workflow failed mid-run or was cancelled, the snapshot would not be updated, producing the same staleness symptom. The snapshot content quality (hasLiveSource=true, hasNonUnknownFeatureData=true) does not rule this out, as those fields reflect the last successful publish.

Less likely — GitHub Pages propagation delay: Even if the workflow ran on time, a GitHub Pages CDN propagation delay could cause the eval to read a stale cached version of status.json. The 3-minute margin makes this plausible but less probable than a scheduling slip.

Least likely — Contract threshold too tight relative to workflow cadence: The feature registry sets staleAfterMinutes=360 for this check, but the expected-output contract enforces maxAgeMinutes=300. If the workflow is scheduled at exactly 300-minute intervals, any minor scheduling jitter will cause the eval to fail. This is a configuration tension, not a runtime failure, but it could explain recurring marginal failures.
